newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: FEATURE - Tiny Slovenia a luminary in global ski market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tiny Slovenia a luminary in global ski market.

text.p: Few ski enthusiasts would be able to pinpoint the tiny Alpine republic of Slovenia on a map.
Even less would know that the former communist country boasts one of the skiing industry's major makers of skis, exporting much of its production to the United States.
But to the two million Slovenians, whose country is exactly half the size of the Netherlands, Elan is as much a part of the national identity as Edam cheese is to the Dutch.
Elan, established in 1945 in the picturesque village of Begunje, was one of Slovenia's most successful firms until 1990 when things suddenly went horribly wrong.
The erstwhile sponsor of Swedish skiing phenomenon Ingemar Stenmark suddenly collapsed because of losses at its savings bank, set up in 1989.
The bank collapsed after promising high interest rates on deposits that far exceeded the level of inflation, which dropped to 550 percent in 1990 from 1,300 percent the year before.
Matters worsened for Elan, which employs 1,300 people, when Slovenia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, subsequently losing around 30 percent of its market.

As a result, 77.25 percent of the then state-owned company was sold to Croatian bank Privredna banka for $21 million. The remaining shares were divided among 78 creditor companies from Croatia and Slovenia.
The sale of Elan caused a political storm in Slovenia, forcing parliament to form a special committee to investigate its bankruptcy and sale due to allegations of corruption and abuse of authority.

Elan fought hard to compensate for the loss of one of its major markets by focusing on countries farther afield. Today it remains one of Slovenia's biggest exporters and is one of the largest employers in the region.

Commanding 80 percent of the domestic ski market, Elan exports 85 percent of its production, the bulk of it downhill, cross-country, ski jumping and snowboard skis, but also boats, gliders, sportswear and other sporting goods.
And the company is now confident it can get rid of its losses and turn in a profit next year on the back of higher sales and a surge in production.

Elan, which also equips the Austrian ski jumping team and Austria's slalom specialist Mario Reiter, expects Alpine ski production to jump 35 percent in 1997 when it takes over two thirds of production -- or around 330,000 skis -- at Austria's Kaestle, now owned by Italy's Benetton group.
"Kaestle chose Elan because of lower wage and production costs, and our modern technology," Bozena Kljucaric, the company's executive vice-president, told Reuters.
Last year, sales rose to $116.1 million from $108.9 million in 1994 and $78.3 million in 1992, but Elan ended 1995 with a loss of $11.1 million, up from a loss of $6.5 million in 1994.

"The loss was mainly a result of $12.4 million of new investments in ski production in 1995, although green winters, which limited sales, and internal technological problems can also be blamed," Kljucaric said.
Elan plans to increase sales substantially to Japan, China, Eastern Europe and South Korea in the next couple of years.
"But the U.S. will remain our most important market, especially after the successful launch of our parabolic skis last year," Kljucaric said.
The U.S. accounts for 30 percent of exports, Japan 24 percent, Canada 18 percent, and Germany 10 percent.

Elan aims to reach a profit of about $3.3 million next year by significantly reducing production waste, operational and material expenses and by meeting its supply targets, Kljucaric said. It expects to post a loss of $2.9 million this year.
